#5224. Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food

Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block said in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.

The report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29.

Food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period.

“Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the company wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy.

Coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73.

Small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent.

Customers also came back. Among Cash App users who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days.

The activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest.

Square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block said zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars.

Block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the company said.

A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%.

Consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% said they would be more likely to pay with bitcoin if it were easier, and 15.7% of that group said they were unsure how it is taxed or regulated.

Block said Congress is weighing a crypto tax package and pointed to a de minimis exemption, which would exempt small gains on qualifying purchases, as one option. Industry groups have pressed lawmakers on crypto tax rules for months, with little movement so far.

The report doesn’t give totals. Block said the number of Square bitcoin payments, the number of sellers receiving them and total bitcoin payment volume are proprietary and not disclosed. Merchant lists like the 425 Los Angeles businesses that accept bitcoin offer a rough sense of reach.

“We think tax policy should account for how people spend bitcoin as well as how they hold it,” Block said.

#5221. Bitcoin miners face a new profitability cliff as difficulty heads for an 8.5% jump

Bitcoin miners face shrinking revenue and tighter electricity margins as a projected difficulty increase threatens less efficient machines.

Bitcoin miners’ expected dollar revenue for the same computing power fell about 6% from Nov. 16 to Nov. 20 in two readings of Luxor’s revenue index.

A difficulty cut had lifted expected Bitcoin earnings earlier in the month, but with the next adjustment now tracking higher, less efficient machines could soon need cheaper electricity to cover their power bills.

Simple Mining’s Nov. 20 reading of Luxor’s hash price index put gross mining revenue at $28.58 per petahash per second (PH/s) per day, with Luxor’s Nov. 16 roundup listing $30.45.

To estimate a machine’s gross daily revenue, multiply the hash price by the machine’s computing power in PH/s. One PH/s equals 1,000 terahashes per second.

The slide also appeared in CloudMineCrypto’s daily series, which estimates revenue from Bitcoin blocks. In its partial Nov. 20 reading, dollar hash price had fallen to about $28.90 from $30.30 per PH/s per day on Nov. 16, while the coin rate held near 0.00047 BTC.

The paired readings explain why a miner can earn roughly the same amount of Bitcoin for a day of work and still have fewer dollars to pay an electricity bill.

Bitcoin’s Nov. 14 adjustment lowered difficulty by 9.13%, from 148.36 trillion to 134.82 trillion. Holding the reward per block steady, the same amount of work could then earn about 10% more Bitcoin. Luxor’s Nov. 16 roundup found that the BTC hash price had risen from 0.00042763 a week earlier to 0.00046839 BTC per PH/s per day.

Over the same period, the dollar hash price fell from $31.95 to $30.45.

The expected coin payout depends on the block subsidy, transaction fees, and how hard it is to find a block. The dollar payout also depends on Bitcoin’s price, since fees accounted for only a small fraction of block rewards in both data sets.

Luxor reported a weekly average of 0.0229 BTC in fees per block on Nov. 16, and the partial Nov. 20 data imply about 0.022 BTC in fees on top of the 3.125 BTC subsidy.

As of Nov. 20, MineOrNot counted 1,008 blocks, halfway to the next adjustment. Blocks were arriving about every nine minutes and 14 seconds, compared with Bitcoin’s ten-minute target.

If that pace persists, MineOrNot estimated difficulty would rise 8.47% to about 146.24 trillion around Nov. 27.

If Bitcoin’s price, the subsidy, and average fees per block stay fixed, an 8.47% rise in difficulty would lower the $28.58 benchmark to about $26.35 per PH/s per day. A 10% increase would put it near $25.98 and bring difficulty almost back to its pre-cut level.

For a machine using 30 joules per terahash, the observed benchmark translates to a power-only break-even rate of 3.97 cents per kilowatt-hour.

With an 8.47% increase in difficulty, the same machine’s ceiling would fall to 3.66 cents. A machine using 13.5 joules per terahash can absorb higher electricity rates, with its ceiling falling from 8.82 cents to 8.13 cents under the same assumptions.

Gross mining revenue can cover a lower electricity rate if difficulty rises 8.47%, even with Bitcoin’s price and block rewards held fixed.

At a hypothetical 3.8¢/kWh, a 30 J/TH rig would stop covering its power bill if difficulty rises 8.47%. The 13.5 J/TH rig would still cover electricity.

Electricity-only model. Excludes pool fees, hosting, hardware and other costs.

Use the November 20 benchmark of $28.58 per PH/s per day. Model the retarget by dividing by 1.0847. At 1 PH/s, the 30 and 13.5 J/TH rigs draw 30 and 13.5 kW. Divide daily gross revenue by 24 times power in kW, multiply by 100, and round to 0.01 cent per kWh.

Electricity-only model. Excludes pool fees, hosting, hardware and other costs.

At a hypothetical electricity rate of 3.8 cents per kWh, the less efficient machine would just cover its power bill at the Nov. 20 benchmark. At that same rate, it would fall short after an 8.47% increase in difficulty. The more efficient machine would cover electricity at that rate in both cases.

The calculation divides gross daily revenue by daily electricity use. A miner at the ceiling has already used all its expected revenue on electricity. Pool fees and any separate hosting charges can lower the rate it can afford, and the operator’s contract and downtime will shape its actual costs.

#5220. Bitcoin Price Crashes to $59,000 as Market Selloff Deepens

The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower.

Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data. The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000.

The break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss.

Wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower.

Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry.

Rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed. Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield.

Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin.

Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027.

JUST IN: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 for the first time since June.BTC is now less than 4% away from a new cycle low 👀 pic.twitter.com/GSZkbGdzZz

Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week.

Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them.

The move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday.

Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session. Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading.

Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13.

Data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure.

The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600.

#5217. U.S. Treasury Secretary Pushes Back on Bigger Fed Hike

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a bigger Federal Reserve rate hike, even as bitcoin broke below $60,000 for the first time since July and stocks sank on bets that the Fed will keep tightening into a selloff.

Bessent told CNBC he would encourage the Fed not to embrace a half-point increase at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. He cited the energy supply shock and a drop in crude prices as reasons for the central bank to hold back.

He argued that one governor now backing a 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year. Bessent said it “seems somewhat peripatetic” to want the bigger increase only 11 or 12 months later. He did not name the governor.

“I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards,” Bessent said.

The comments came two days after Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC a half-point hike is probably necessary in December and that the central bank may need to “shock people.” Waller said inflation is “headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”

Waller is not alone. Minutes of the October meeting showed nearly all officials expect a quarter-point hike in December, and two floated a larger one. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also declined to rule out a bigger move on Thursday.

“We’ve now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress,” Goolsbee told reporters. “So everything’s always on the table.”

Not everyone wants to go bigger. New York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.” St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027.

The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years and held them steady in October. Inflation has stayed hot since the Iran strikes pushed up energy prices earlier this year.

Citi still expects a quarter-point increase in December. Global chief economist Nathan Sheets said Thursday he does not see a need for 50 basis points despite persistent inflation. In a note Friday, the bank wrote that “Fed officials will consequently have little appetite to hike into an equity sell-off.”

Citi expects the Fed to hold after December and begin cutting later in 2027. Traders agree on the next step: the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point hike, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 10 basis points to 4.95% as investors bought bonds.

Stocks fell for another day. The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 2% in morning trading, and the VIX volatility index topped 30, its highest level since March.

Bitcoin traded near $59,700 shortly before 11 a.m. ET, down more than 5% on the day, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro. It broke below $60,000 for the first time since early July and is on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2022.

Higher rates are a headwind for assets that pay no yield, and the selloff has reached companies that hold bitcoin. Strategy’s stock fell for a sixth straight session on Thursday, and the bitcoin price has dropped roughly 25% in a month, a slide Bitcoin Magazine tracked earlier this week.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill tied the outlook to inflation in a note dated Nov. 18. “Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he said.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,300.

Binance’s base reward rate for holding Ripple USD (RLUSD) rose from 4.48% to an annualized 6.37% for the seven days through Nov. 20.

At a steady qualifying balance of 10,000 RLUSD, the estimated weekly payout rose from 8.25 XRP to 12.72 XRP as the exchange also used a lower price to convert the reward into XRP.

A separate 600,000 XRP rewards campaign began at 00:00 UTC on Nov. 20. The new round runs through Dec. 18 and gives eligible customers a reason to keep more RLUSD on Binance.

Binance’s distribution table shows base APRs of 4.84% on Oct. 30 and 5.29% on Nov. 6, with XRP conversion references of $1.2379 and $1.2072 for those payouts. The base rate fell to 4.48% on Nov. 13, with a $1.0413 reference, before climbing to 6.37% on Nov. 20 as the reference dropped to $0.9603.

On a constant qualifying balance of 10,000 RLUSD, Binance’s seven-day formula estimates rewards of $9.28, $10.15, $8.59, and $12.22 across the four weeks before conversion.

Dividing by each week’s reference and rounding down to two decimal places gives 7.49, 8.40, 8.25 and 12.72 XRP.

Each column is the annualized base APR Binance reported for the seven days ending on that distribution date, excluding reward multipliers.

The estimated payout rose about 54% in XRP from the third week to the fourth. The higher base rate increased the dollar value under the formula, and the lower conversion price turned each dollar of reward into more XRP.

Users qualify through net RLUSD balances in eligible Spot, Funding, Flexible Earn, or Margin accounts. For each day, Binance uses the lowest balance it finds in hourly snapshots, then averages those daily lows over seven days.

Eligible participants generally receive XRP in their main Spot account. The formula rewards maintaining a balance through the week because a low reading counts for the entire day.

The renewal also applies a 1.1x boost to eligible RLUSD in Flexible Earn and 1.2x to qualifying balance increases above a baseline from the prior two weeks. The portion that meets both tests can earn 1.3 times the base reward.

#5214. Hill, Moreno blame delays for missed Clarity Act window but differ on reach of agency rulemaking

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Moreno says agencies can deliver 80% of a crypto framework, while Hill warns rulemaking cannot replace lasting legislation.

Rep. French Hill and Sen. Bernie Moreno said Congress missed a chance to pass the Clarity Act while momentum from the GENIUS Act was strong, but offered different assessments of how much regulators can accomplish while market structure legislation remains stalled.

Speaking in separate interviews on Thursday at The Hill and The Block's Capitol Crypto Forum, Hill argued that agency action cannot provide the permanent legal certainty that legislation would. Moreno said regulators could deliver much of the framework themselves, though he acknowledged legislation is the ideal route.

"I’m a little bit more bullish than French," Moreno said. "I think it can accomplish 80% through a very rigorous rulemaking process that can’t be unwound."

The Ohio senator added that the Securities and Exchange Commission and Commodity Futures Trading Commission should use the next two years to establish rules that would make it difficult for a future administration to undo.

"Is that the right way to do it? No," he added. "I think the right way to do it is Congress should pass the Clarity Act."

Hill, the Arkansas Republican who also chairs the House Financial Services Committee, said since the Clarity Act's failure, regulators have mostly followed in the footsteps and goals of market structure proposals. But he added that their authority is limited.

"My argument is it’s not a permanent fix. It is subject to litigation. It does not have the force of law," Hill said.

Both Hill and Moreno said it was a mistake to advance the GENIUS Act separately from Clarity, which passed the House but stalled out after a failed Senate vote in September.

"I urged the Senate and the administration last summer to have Clarity and GENIUS passed together in the House," Hill said. "And I still stand by that."

Moreno, a former car dealer, gave a sales analogy for the breakdown.

"Time kills all deals," he said, adding that lawmakers failed to capitalize on momentum from the stablecoin legislation.

"The bill started at 300 pages, ended up at 600 pages," Moreno said.

Neither had much hope for passage during the lame-duck session. Asked what was realistically possible to achieve over the coming weeks, Moreno answered: "Zero. Zero."

Hill was slightly more optimistic, saying lawmakers "never give up hope in a lame duck," though "the chances are not high."

Hill said it was a good sign that Rep. Maxine Waters pointed out digital asset market structure as an issue she intended to address if she's elected as committee chair.

Moreno also said bipartisan negotiations were not off the table, while blaming earlier talks for being "tornadoed" in disputes over President Donald Trump and ethics.

He said he would consider restarting negotiations with the House-passed legislation.

"By the time we got to September with the Senate version, it was just very, very, very complicated," Moreno said.

Hill argued that Congress still needs to finish the job: "To have GENIUS but not market structure is a huge mistake."

#5212. Researchers Publish Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum SHRINCS Proposal

Several researchers have published a 131-page security analysis of SHRINCS, a proposed post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin, and are asking the wider community to look for flaws in it. Researcher Mikhail Kudinov announced the first version Thursday in a thread on X, saying the paper reduces SHRINCS’ security to the properties of its underlying hash function.

The analysis, dated Nov. 18, estimates classical security of 121.4 to 122.7 bits for SHRINCS, though those figures rest on assumptions that include three unproven conjectures. Kudinov said the work is not finished. The team is still working on a new analysis of a property called SM-DSPR, whose bound has so far been conjectured, and on tightening a reprogramming step and improving a bound against quantum attackers.

SHRINCS is a hash-based scheme, meaning its security rests on hash functions rather than the elliptic curve math behind today’s Bitcoin signatures. It places two designs under one key: a stateful part built on FXMSS with WOTS+C, and a stateless fallback built on SLH-DSA. Because both use the same hash function, Kudinov said, the proof has to cover both.

Signature size is the main cost. Under the draft proposal, stateful SHRINCS signatures run from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while the stateless fallback is 5,777 bytes. Schnorr signatures on Bitcoin today are 64 bytes, and ECDSA signatures typically come in around 71. Signatures take up scarce block space, so larger ones mean fewer transactions per block.

The compact stateful path carries a danger. It relies on one-time keys, and if a wallet accidentally reuses one, an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal the funds. Wallet software therefore has to track the state of every key. The stateless path avoids the problem, but at a much larger size.

Jonas Nick, Blockstream’s director of research, told Isabel Foxen Duke, head of the MARA Foundation, on MARA Foundation TV that wallets must automatically fall back to the stateless path whenever a state counter could be compromised. “It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” he said. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”

Nick also warned that heavy use of the larger signatures would weigh on the network. “We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very big signatures,” he said. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”

The authors are clear that the analysis needs scrutiny. Kudinov said it has not been sufficiently peer reviewed, and the project’s GitHub repository warns that the documents may contain errors and should not be the sole basis for deploying SHRINCS. “We tried to be careful, but a proof of this size can have mistakes,” he wrote, asking readers to open an issue if they find one.

The team also produced two results that are not specific to SHRINCS: a classical bound for a property called ITSR without reprogramming, and a quadratic quantum bound for undetectability. Kudinov said they also apply to SPHINCS+ and SLH-DSA, the hash-based schemes SHRINCS borrows from, and that they were published as separate papers.

The SHRINCS work lands as quantum risk climbs the agenda. A global securities regulators’ group this week warned that moving blockchains to quantum-resistant cryptography may be especially hard, and researchers recently built a post-quantum defense for the Lightning Network after Bitcoin’s first quantum-safe transaction was shown without a fork.

The draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal for SHRINCS is also open for comment. “We need all the possible feedback — engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, said of it. “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.”

Bitcoin fell as low as $62k late Saturday, its sixth straight weekly decline. Meanwhile, tokenized stocks crossed $4 billion in onchain value for the first time on Nov 11. Tokenized stocks are now roughly five times their value on January 1.

Tokenized stocks track equity prices, not crypto, so a falling BTC doesn’t directly pull their prices down. What stands out, however, is that crypto users appear to keep buying them through the selloff. Demand for 24/7 trading and onchain access to US equities appears to have found strong product-market fit as they are holding up even as the rest of the crypto market weakens.

In September, rising share prices drove most of the growth in value of tokenized stocks. Since mid-October, new minting has driven the growth in value even as share prices dropped. Over the eleven weeks to Nov 13, minting added $1.12 billion while price moves took away $339 million. Binance’s bStocks accounted for about four fifths of that minting, led by NVIDIA, SpaceX and Circle.

Market value has stalled over the past two weeks. We expect minting to pick back up again with the launch of OKXICE on Nov 23 opening large-cap tokenized stocks to US retail.

Securitize reported $11.5 million in tokenization revenue in Q3, its highest on record and 28% more than Q3 2025. Securitize's average tokenized assets reached a record $5 billion as of Q3 as BlackRock, Ark Invest and Neuberger brought new products onchain.

Tokenization revenue is more variable because it rises and falls with issuance, while asset servicing has settled around $7 million a quarter. Securitize's acquisition of River One could help smooth out those revenue swings and diversify its top line. Lending against tokenized assets adds recurring income on top of issuance. We expect credit to show up as Securitize's third revenue line within a year of the deal closing.

Most of the roughly $4 billion of tokenized stock sits in wrappers that US investors can't buy. Only about 10% is open to American investors, and almost all of that is crypto companies including Securitize, Figure, Exodus and Forward Industries. NVIDIA, SpaceX and the other large names are effectively offshore only.

That could change on Nov 23, when OKXICE opens to US customers who have onboarded through its CeDeFi Wallet. It’s the first venue built for American retail at scale, so the onshore share should grow post-launch. We expect issuer-backed listings to drive it, with 67 companies having opted out.

#5207. SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme

The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.

The agency said Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022. A federal court granted a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze and expedited discovery to halt what the SEC called an ongoing scheme.

Federal prosecutors in New York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases. The SEC and CFTC suits were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, and the CFTC said the court has appointed Kevin B. Duff as temporary receiver to take control of the companies and the individual defendants’ assets.

According to the SEC’s complaint, Williams and Johnson sold limited partnership interests in private funds through a network of promoters, including to Williams’s former investment advisory clients. They promised a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm that supposedly returned at least 6% every month by trading foreign exchange.

Investor money, the pitch went, would first be converted into a crypto asset and then used for that arbitrage. The complaint does not name bitcoin as the asset. It says about $109 million of the roughly $210 million raised from July 2022 to September 2025 was sent to the fund’s Coinbase account and converted.

Of that, more than $56 million went to personal crypto accounts held by Williams, Johnson and a relief defendant, according to the complaint. About $40 million ended up on three platforms where some of it was used to trade other crypto assets, but little to no money was used to trade FX. After October 2025, the scheme raised about $350 million, and none of it was sent to Coinbase.

The SEC said the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi payments to earlier investors and moved more than $220 million to themselves. The money paid for exotic cars, expensive homes, private air travel and other businesses they owned, and helped feed Johnson’s gambling. Promoters took more than $50 million.

Anderson is accused of producing fake financial reports, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report from a supposedly independent firm. The SEC said the documents falsely claimed the returns had been verified against bank and brokerage records. It said Anderson did no audit work, was not independent and had a financial stake in the scheme.

Prosecutors in Manhattan charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The FBI arrested Williams in Kokomo, Indiana, and Johnson in Gilbert, Arizona, on Wednesday. Prosecutors put the total raised at more than $600 million.

“As alleged, Phillip Patrick Williams and Devin Allen Johnson promised to use investor funds for profitable foreign exchange currency trading,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Williams and Johnson instead stole hundreds of millions of dollars from their investors for personal expenses and to pay off earlier investors in a Ponzi-like fashion.”

The CFTC put the Ponzi at more than $550 million from at least 2,100 participants and said defendants kept soliciting money through at least October 2026. Its complaint seeks restitution, disgorgement, civil penalties, trading bans and a permanent injunction. The SEC is seeking injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties.

The case follows other recent enforcement actions tied to crypto-branded fraud. The SEC charged two companies in a $130 million crypto trading scheme last month, and New York sought a $1.37 billion judgment against the operators of the NovaTech Ponzi scheme. In August, the CFTC charged Goliath Ventures with a $400 million bitcoin fraud.

Anne McKinley, acting associate director of the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office, said the promise of “a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money.”

#5206. Fluidkey’s $1.6 million hack exposes a security risk even when private keys never leave users’ devices

Sending funds requires an app update, and users who spot an unfamiliar transfer can look up their own receiving address or transaction hash on the relevant blockchain.

The company announced the return of its web, iOS, and Android apps in v1.79.22. It said older versions would stay offline and told users to open Settings and select Update to re-enable transactions.

Fluidkey attributed the incident to flaws in a third-party logging tool and said users’ private keys stayed on their devices, and said it took services offline on Nov. 19. In its update that evening, it said it had seen no further unauthorized transactions since the shutdown and was working with SEAL 911 to investigate and trace funds.

Its initial warning to avoid the site and app came before the new version was available.

Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery traced roughly $1.6 million in payouts to wallets it linked to the incident across six chains, including Base and Ethereum.

The independent Fluidkey drain tracker, maintained by pepebndc, put the total near $1.63 million across seven chains in its Nov. 20 morning snapshot. That estimate includes suspected destinations and excludes likely owner withdrawals.

Bitquery says the tracker labeled one Polygon payout as an owner withdrawal, linking it to the incident after following the recipient’s activity on Base.

The firm also separated the incident-linked payments from about $349,000 sent to wallets with an established history during its hour-long scan.

That group includes ordinary payments before the drain and about $277,000 sent during it to an older wallet across Ethereum and Base. Bitquery interpreted the latter as one user moving their own funds, and left another $65,000 unclassified.

Fluidkey’s standing recovery guide describes SARA as a last-resort option for verifying addresses or accessing funds. It warns that moving funds outside the regular app may impair app functionality.

In its incident update, Fluidkey said it would contact affected users individually and publish a full post-mortem. It warned about impersonation and said its staff would never contact users privately through social media, and directed users to its official website for support.

#5204. CFTC Chair Selig outlines how Hyperliquid and other onchain venues could enter the US

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Onchain venues looking to offer derivatives to U.S. retail traders would need to register as an exchange or partner with a registered one, Selig said.

Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig said crypto onchain platforms looking to offer derivatives to U.S. retail traders can register as an exchange or partner with one that is already registered.

Selig was asked how a decentralized platform like Hyperliquid could enter the U.S. during an interview Thursday at The Hill and The Block's Capitol Crypto Forum. He pointed to Backpack, which earlier this week received three licenses for its U.S. entry, as an example of the first route. Other platforms are pursuing partnerships with registered firms, Selig said.

"You're going to have to come in and partner with an exchange or obtain your own exchange, which doesn't change the ability and the great features of crypto and blockchain," Selig said.

Backpack's three licenses include Futures Commission Merchant (FCM), Designated Contract Market (DCM), and Derivatives Clearing Organization (DCO). "Together, the three licenses provide the full regulatory stack for Backpack's U.S. entry, the first by a crypto-native exchange offering leveraged perpetual futures with global unified liquidity," Backpack said earlier this week.

Selig said platforms can continue using onchain technology, but they would still have to follow the same rules as other exchanges.

Selig also said the CFTC would work with the Justice Department when states sue federally registered platforms in an effort to challenge the agency's jurisdiction. The CFTC and the U.S. government had already sued Utah together in October, and the agency filed separate lawsuits against Arkansas and Louisiana on Nov. 13.

"If it's a legal and lawful derivative, it should be regulated by the market regulator. It's not something that goes to the state," Selig said.

Selig distinguished derivatives exchanges from casinos and state-licensed gambling venues, saying the CFTC has no business regulating the latter. On event contracts, Selig said the CFTC checks whether they are derivatives and meet its rules, including whether they can be easily manipulated. He said the agency's proposed Rule 40.11 lists the public policy factors it would consider when reviewing these contracts.

Selig said just because a single-stock perpetual contract has no expiry date does not make it a security-based swap. He said the structure of these contracts matters and compared their daily funding payments to variation margin payments on other futures contracts.

"It doesn't have an expiration date. And so there's what's called a funding rate, where payments are exchanged on a daily basis," Selig said. "This is very similar to variation margin with other types of futures contracts. But they're structured as futures contracts; they're not structured as a swap or as a security-based swap."

#5199. Ripple’s Alderoty doubts Elizabeth Warren will ‘set crypto policy in this country,’ backs durable agency rules

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Alderoty downplayed Warren’s influence, backing durable agency rules, and urging crypto groups to unify their message to Congress.

Ripple Chief Legal Officer Stuart Alderoty is looking to federal regulators to carry crypto market rules over the finish line, arguing that Elizabeth Warren's expected rise to lead the Senate Banking Committee won't put her in charge of the industry's future.

"I don’t think Elizabeth Warren is going to set crypto policy in this country," Alderoty said at The Hill and The Block’s Capitol Crypto Forum on Thursday. "She'll probably focus on oversight and hearings, which I think will be a short-term distraction."

Alderoty, who also serves as president of the National Cryptocurrency Association, said he expects other lawmakers to take the wheel on crypto policy over Warren, who he described as "overtly anti-crypto."

Despite this, he does not expect a version of the Clarity Act to be reintroduced in the coming Congress, pointing to a packed legislative calendar and the 2028 presidential election as priorities.

Pieces of the proposal could be folded into tax legislation or other bills, he said, but a broader bill would likely struggle to garner the committee support needed to reach the floor.

"I think the emphasis and the focus is going to move to the SEC and the CFTC," Alderoty said, also mentioning collaborations with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Asked whether action from those agencies would be enough for the industry over the next two years without market structure legislation, Alderoty said: "I think it's enough, and I think it's really important."

He argues that rules created through public comment and data analysis would be difficult for a future administration to reverse because they would need to carry out their own policymaking and justify disrupting the market's reliance on the existing rules, he said.

Alderoty contrasted that with the approach taken by former SEC Chair Gary Gensler, arguing that reliance on enforcement left little to no durable policy when he left.

"The Gensler SEC did not do the hard work of rulemaking," he said. "What they decided to do was fall back to regulation by enforcement."

"This administration is doing the hard work of rulemaking, and that is durable," he added.

Alderoty also pushed crypto companies to improve how they present their priorities to Congress.

He cited a handful of possible reasons for the breakdown in the Clarity Act's passage, including the Senate's decision not to advance the House-passed bill, the schism between stablecoin and market structure legislation and disputes over rewards. Ethics concerns surrounding the Trump family’s crypto ties ultimately "overwhelmed the conversation," he said.

The industry's competing messages also made things murky, he added, with different groups and companies all going after lawmakers with "esoteric issues" on DeFi, stablecoin rewards, and token classifications.

When you consider that lawmakers' understanding of crypto can vary widely, it makes the industry's more technical pitches hard to follow. Alderoty likened the situation to a policymaker telling him about fishermen coming in to discuss fishing laws, tackle and tides that the lawmaker didn't understand.

"We need to do the hard work of seeing what do we agree on, making that clear," Alderoty said.

Despite the setbacks, he urged the industry to continue working across party lines.

"Crypto is a policy issue," Alderoty said. "It's not a political issue."

#5198. Sky offers nearly 30% yield but 99.96% of its lending vault is unavailable for immediate withdrawals

Sky’s stUSDS vault had just 0.04% of assets available for withdrawal, leaving savers dependent on loan repayments or new deposits.

Sky’s stUSDS lending vault had $60,484 worth of USDS available for immediate withdrawals at 17:50 UTC on Nov. 20, about 0.04% of the vault’s $161.6 million in total assets, according to Spark.

Spark’s dashboard showed about $161.5 million in USDS out on loan at the time, and those loans account for nearly all of the vault’s reported value.

A holder could redeem only from the portion available in USDS. For example, a saver with $100,000 worth of stUSDS could not have redeemed that entire position directly at the time of the reading, even if nobody else withdrew first.

Savers deposit USDS and receive stUSDS tokens representing their position, and the pool lends USDS to borrowers who put up SKY tokens as collateral. Spark’s dashboard displayed a 29.74% annual percentage yield at the time.

Sky explains that the yield varies with lending conditions. Funds in use earn a rate tied to what borrowers pay, and unused USDS earns the Sky Savings Rate.

The Spark reading measures withdrawal liquidity across the entire vault.

Larger direct withdrawals may have to wait for more USDS to enter the lending pool.

The withdrawal figure is a point-in-time reading. The diagram shows possible inflows without estimating their timing or amount.

Divide the $60,484 of withdrawal liquidity by $161,583,152 of total vault assets and multiply by 100. The result is 0.03743%, rounded to 0.04%. The connectors show possible sources of liquidity described by Sky.

The withdrawal figure is a point-in-time reading. The diagram shows possible inflows without estimating their timing or amount.

When borrowers repay, the USDS they return can become available for withdrawals. New deposits can also add USDS to the pool before borrowers pay down their loans.

When nearly all of the pool is already lent out, a holder may have to wait for more USDS to come in before redeeming their full position.

Sky says the module has no mechanism to liquidate borrowers early to free up funds for depositors. The loan collateral is in SKY, while holders redeem their stUSDS shares for USDS available in the vault.

Sky Frontier Foundation separately said on Nov. 20 that users exchanged more than $2 billion of USDS for USDC the previous day through Sky’s Peg Stability Module. The foundation said the facility continued to swap the two stablecoins at a one-to-one rate during the Nov. 19 activity.

The swap facility serves users who already have USDS to exchange. An stUSDS holder using the vault would first have to redeem for USDS before using that route to get USDC.

The amount a vault depositor can withdraw depends on how much USDS is in the lending pool when the redemption is attempted.

#5196. Bitcoin Price Slips to Lows Not Seen Since 2024, Nasdaq Plunges 5%

The bitcoin price slid to near $58,300 on Friday afternoon, down about 6.2% over the past 24 hours, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, as a deepening selloff in chip and artificial intelligence stocks sent the Nasdaq down about 5% and pushed bitcoin just under its summer low.

Bitcoin broke below $60,000 late Friday morning, a few hours after this morning’s report had it near $61,500. Over the past 24 hours, the bitcoin price has traded between $57,655 and $62,562, a drop of about $3,880. Bitcoin is down about 25% in November, on pace for its worst month since June 2022.

Selling on Wall Street sped up through the afternoon. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5% in late trading and the S&P 500 dropped about 3.5%. Yahoo Finance said the Nasdaq was on pace to close negative for the year, while the S&P 500 was poised to close in correction territory.

Chipmakers led the drop. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 12.5% to near $128, and AMD, Broadcom and Micron also posted double-digit losses. Gold futures dropped nearly 5%. Treasury yields fell as traders rotated into bonds and defensive sectors such as consumer staples and healthcare, Reuters reported.

Anthropic (ANT) fell nearly 12% to around $86 on its first full day of trading, leaving it just above its $83 IPO price. The stock had closed its Thursday debut at $97.17 after raising $81.3 billion in the largest IPO of all time, CNBC reported.

Leveraged traders were forced out as the bitcoin price broke support. About $1.53 billion in crypto bets were wiped out over 24 hours, with long positions making up $1.4 billion of that total. Bitcoin alone accounted for around $540 million, while ether fell more than 8% to around $1,600.

Bitcoin funds have been sellers, too. Investors have pulled roughly $3.5 billion from U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs so far this month, including $582 million on Thursday. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $541.1 million of Thursday’s withdrawals, its largest one-day outflow on record.

Rate worries are adding pressure. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a half-point Federal Reserve hike in December. Traders still saw a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point increase, and some strategists warned that further hikes could deepen the selloff.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said the drop looks driven more by the AI stock selloff than by problems inside crypto. Bitcoin has increasingly traded alongside other growth assets that depend on easy money, he said.

The dip to $57,655 briefly took bitcoin just under its summer low near $57,700. It is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, its longest losing streak since 2022.

Strategy (MSTR) fell about 8.4% to near $78.90, adding to the losses after the stock fell for a sixth straight day on Thursday. Coinbase (COIN) dropped about 5.5% to near $103. Robinhood (HOOD) lost about 9.6% and Circle (CRCL) fell about 7.9%.

Bitcoin miners fared worst. MARA Holdings (MARA) sank about 17% to near $5.17, IREN (IREN) fell about 17% and CleanSpark (CLSK) dropped about 16%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 8.4%, and Galaxy Digital (GLXY) fell about 9.4%. Many miners have expanded into AI data centers, tying their shares to the chip selloff.

The bitcoin price is now down more than 50% from its record above $126,000, set in October 2025.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $58,300.

#5194. Kalshi’s Quintenz says insider trading is ‘just easier to see’ in prediction markets than stocks

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Kalshi board member Brian Quintenz said there are far more insider trading cases in the stock market, but the link between a trader and an event's outcome can be easier to see in prediction markets.

Brian Quintenz, Kalshi board member and former commissioner of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, said there are far more insider trading cases in the stock market than in prediction markets, where it can be easier to see when someone has affected the outcome of an event they traded on.

"And there are by far more insider trading cases that happen in the stock market than anything that happens in the derivatives markets or in the prediction market space," Quintenz said Thursday at The Hill and The Block's Capitol Crypto Forum. "It's just easier to see because it's very direct."

Quintenz said the possibility of insider trading should not make a market illegal or invalid. He said enforcement after a violation should supplement the work exchanges do to prevent it, and added that there was more work to do.

Dan Berkovitz, vice chair of external and regulatory affairs at Millennium Management and a former CFTC commissioner, said federal and exchange rules already prohibit insider trading. He said exchanges also need rules on who can trade, including employees of organizations involved in a contract and people who can influence its outcome.

"So you need rules against insider trading, you need participation limits, and you need strict anti-manipulation provisions," Berkovitz said.

Berkovitz pointed to mention markets, where the outcome can depend on whether a person says a particular word or phrase. A person who can decide whether to say something can also decide the outcome of the contract, he said. Berkovitz welcomed the CFTC's guidance but said more work is needed on who has insider information or can influence the outcome.

"Who has influence or control of the contract? Who has insider knowledge? Those types of things, I think we can still use further development, but there's initial steps being taken to get there," Berkovitz said.

Christy Goldsmith Romero, senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former CFTC commissioner, said exchanges are the first line of defense against insider trading and that the CFTC probably needs to do more. She pointed to the requirement that exchanges certifying their own contracts attest that those contracts are not readily susceptible to manipulation. She added that greater clarity was needed from the CFTC to assist exchanges with that.

Quintenz agreed that more guidance would help. However, he said whether a contract is readily susceptible to manipulation is a judgment call and that the CFTC should explain how it applies the standard rather than leaving exchanges to come up with different standards on their own.

The panel also discussed who should regulate sports event contracts. Berkovitz explained that the post-Dodd-Frank final rule continues to prohibit gaming contracts via the CFTC, subject only to future regulatory amendment. The latest interim rule, however, draws a distinction between gambling conducted at a casino and products listed for trading on a federally regulated exchange, Berkovitz said. He added that a legal question remains over whether essentially the same product can be treated as a swap on one platform but not another.

Quintenz said he had submitted a comment letter in his personal capacity, noting that the Supreme Court's 2018 sports betting ruling did not give states exclusive authority. He said federal regulators can oversee exchanges and states can continue regulating casinos and sportsbooks.

Meanwhile, Goldsmith Romero said the Supreme Court would likely take up the matter given the conflicting decisions across the Circuit Courts. "I think it's likely that the prediction markets may end up losing on the sports contracts," she said.

She also said the Securities and Exchange Commission could become more involved as prediction markets offer more contracts related to public companies and their stocks. She added that it would also help if both the SEC and CFTC worked together to provide more clarity.

#5191. Coinbase backs CFTC proposal to distinguish prediction market contracts from gambling

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Coinbase said event contracts already qualify as swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act and that explicit inclusion would provide greater regulatory certainty.

Crypto exchange Coinbase has filed comments supporting the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission's proposals to explicitly include event contracts in the definition of a "swap" and separate them from casino-style gambling products, as federal regulators and states remain locked in legal disputes over jurisdiction of prediction markets.

In a letter submitted Wednesday, Coinbase said that event contracts — including contracts based on sports, politics, culture, and weather — already qualify as swaps under the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

The company argued that event contracts are tradeable financial instruments whose value and payment depend on future events, and that they can help market participants "hedge real economic risks."

"Making that treatment explicit will provide important certainty in an area where state actions and conflicting judicial decisions have created unnecessary confusion," the company said.

In a separate letter, Coinbase backed the CFTC's interim rule to exclude casino-style gambling products from the "swap" definition. The company said such gambling products are neither tradable nor cleared and were "never indicated" by Congress to fall within the definition of swap.

"Casino games and sportsbook wagers are not derivatives, and they have long been regulated by the states and tribes," the company added.

Coinbase argued that exchange-traded event contracts are "fundamentally distinct" from sportsbooks traditionally regulated under state laws.

"An event-contract exchange serves as a neutral market operator," the company said. "[It] does not choose prices or act as a counterparty to its members' trades, and it is indifferent to whether any given customer wins or loses."

Coinbase's comments were in response to the CFTC's proposal and interim final rule released last month, which were open for public comment through Nov. 18.

Federal regulators and state authorities have been embroiled in escalating legal battles over who has the authority to regulate prediction market platforms. The CFTC has maintained that it has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction markets under the CEA, while several states have argued that certain event contracts violate state gambling laws.

During a Thursday interview at The Hill and The Block's Capitol Crypto Forum, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said the CFTC would work with the Justice Department to defend its jurisdiction when states sue prediction market platforms.

The CFTC and the DOJ sued Utah last month and filed lawsuits against Arkansas and Louisiana last week.

"If it's a legal and lawful derivative, it should be regulated by the market regulator. It's not something that goes to the state," Selig said.

#5187. IOSCO warns quantum upgrades could slow blockchains, leave security gaps

A Solana test network ran about 90% slower with quantum-resistant signatures, and wallets that keep using older keys could remain vulnerable.

The International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) warned that upgrading blockchains to withstand quantum attacks could slow transactions and raise fees.

In a report released Thursday, IOSCO said some quantum-resistant digital signatures take up far more space than those used to authorize transactions today. Larger signatures mean fewer transactions can fit in each block, which could increase congestion, push up fees and require more storage.

IOSCO cited an experiment in which a test version of Solana ran about 90% slower with quantum-resistant signatures.

No known quantum computer can break the cryptography that secures these networks today. IOSCO urged firms to start preparing now because the transition could take years.

IOSCO said layer-1 networks use cryptography both to authorize transactions and to reach agreement on which blocks to add. Even after an upgrade, funds in dormant wallets and applications could remain vulnerable if they still rely on older keys.

Layer-2 networks can use quantum-resistant proofs to verify transactions and still depend on vulnerable systems to settle those transactions, move assets between chains or approve upgrades.

In April, Bitcoin advocate Samson Mow warned that larger post-quantum signatures could reduce Bitcoin’s throughput and that rushed fixes might introduce new vulnerabilities.

In October, Starknet’s community backed research into becoming an independent, quantum-resistant layer-1 network, following concerns over its reliance on Ethereum’s security upgrade timeline.

Ethereum researcher Justin Drake has since outlined a 2028 post-quantum transition target, ahead of the network’s existing 2029 roadmap.

#5182. Michael Saylor sees up to $7.5 billion in ‘natural demand’ for Strategy’s STRC preferred stock

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Saylor said the credit-market contraction began around May, and the company is responding by reducing the amount of STRC outstanding until it reaches an equilibrium level.

Strategy Strategy, Inc. (MSTR) Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said "natural, organic" demand for the company's STRC preferred stock at its current 12% dividend rate is likely between $5 billion and $7.5 billion.

"I don't know exactly where the number is, but I’m going to go out on a limb and say that somewhere between $5 billion and $7.5 billion, there is natural organic demand to hold the instrument at 12% dividend," Saylor said during a live investor Q&A on Thursday.

His comments come as Strategy has been actively repurchasing STRC shares at prices below its $100 stated level. President and CEO Phong Le said the company has bought back about $3 billion of the preferred stock at prices between $95 and $99, below the issuance price level.

Saylor described the current environment as a credit-market contraction that began around May. He said the company is responding by reducing the amount of STRC outstanding until it reaches an equilibrium level that the market will support at the existing dividend rate.

"We're going to contract the outstanding STRC because 12% is a fat dividend for an investment-grade instrument,” Saylor said. "As we buy it back, we lengthen the duration, we strip the risk, we improve the credit."

CEO Le also said that the recent buybacks have de-risked the company's balance sheet after credit markets tightened over the past four to five months. Le added that Strategy had previously expanded STRC from an initial $2.5 billion issuance to roughly $8 billion under favorable market conditions.

Saylor framed the support for STRC as important for the long-term credibility of the product. He compared it to an insurance company paying claims, arguing that failing to back the security in a weaker market would damage confidence among credit investors over multiple years.

"When the company is swapping either BTC or MSTR for STRC, we're supporting the credit, we're supporting the brand of the company, we're improving the product quality," Saylor said.

The Strategy Chairman also reiterated that the company has at least three years' worth of cash right now, so it will still be able to operate even if the current bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) downturn continues.

The world's largest digital asset treasury firm owned 850,849 BTC as of Nov. 15, according to its latest disclosure, which amounts to more than 4% of bitcoin's maximum supply cap. Last month, holders of Strategy's STRC, STRF, STRK and STRD preferred shares approved a change allowing dividends to accrue daily, rather than on the previous schedule.

Last week, the company sold approximately $244.7 million in MSTR shares to fund bitcoin purchases and STRC repurchases.
